concepts.name: Earth's Axial Tilt: Cause and Consequences
key_dimensions: Exact angle of tilt (23.5°) and its reference plane (plane of ecliptic)
Why axial tilt — NOT distance from Sun — is the primary cause of seasons (common UPSC trap)
Consequences if tilt were 0° (no seasons) vs. 90° (extreme seasons)
Relationship between axial tilt and the obliquity cycle (Milankovitch)

concepts.name: Perihelion and Aphelion: Earth-Sun Distance Paradox
key_dimensions: Exact dates: Perihelion (~Jan 3) and Aphelion (~Jul 4) and their orbital significance
The paradox: Earth is closest to Sun during Northern Hemisphere winter — why seasons still occur
Effect of slightly greater solar energy at perihelion on Southern Hemisphere summer intensity
Distinction between orbital eccentricity (Milankovitch) and axial tilt as seasonal drivers

concepts.name: Solstices: Summer and Winter — Astronomical and Climatic Significance
key_dimensions: Exact dates (June 21 & December 22), subsolar point positions (Tropic of Cancer & Capricorn)
Longest/shortest day concept and its reversal between hemispheres — a classic trap question
Altitude of the Sun at noon on solstice dates at different latitudes
Cultural and traditional significance vs. meteorological season start dates

concepts.name: Equinoxes: Equal Day-Night and Their Exceptions
key_dimensions: March 21 (Vernal) and September 23 (Autumnal) — subsolar point at the equator
Why day and night are NOT exactly 12 hours each on equinox (atmospheric refraction trap)
Difference between astronomical equinox and meteorological equal-day concept
Equinox as the basis for defining the celestial equator and declination of the Sun

concepts.name: Angle of Incidence and Insolation: Latitudinal Variation
key_dimensions: Why tropical regions receive more insolation — perpendicular rays vs. oblique rays
Spreading effect of oblique rays over larger surface area reducing intensity
Longer atmospheric path for oblique rays increasing absorption and scattering
Relationship with altitude angle of the Sun and seasonal temperature variation

concepts.name: Duration of Daylight: Variation with Latitude and Season
key_dimensions: Poles experiencing 6-month day and 6-month night — the 'Midnight Sun' and 'Polar Night'
Circle of illumination and its shifting position relative to Earth's axis
At Arctic/Antarctic Circle (66.5°N/S): one day of 24-hour daylight/darkness per year
Equatorial regions having nearly constant 12-hour days throughout the year

concepts.name: Seasons in the Northern vs. Southern Hemisphere: Mirror Image Concept
key_dimensions: When NH has summer, SH has winter — exact reversal and its implications for agriculture/climate
Southern Hemisphere seasons being slightly more intense due to perihelion coinciding with SH summer
Why the concept of 'universal seasons' is misleading — equatorial regions have no distinct seasons
UPSC trap: identifying correct season for a given hemisphere from a given date

concepts.name: Tropical, Temperate, and Polar Zones: Definition by Solar Geometry
key_dimensions: Tropics defined by the subsolar point range (23.5°N to 23.5°S) — receives direct overhead Sun
Polar circles (66.5°N/S) defined by the threshold for midnight sun phenomenon
Temperate zones as transitional — no overhead Sun, no midnight Sun
Overlap trap: Regions near Tropic boundaries experience near-overhead Sun but not exactly overhead

concepts.name: Kepler's Second Law and Orbital Velocity: Seasonal Length Inequality
key_dimensions: Earth moves faster at perihelion and slower at aphelion (equal areas in equal times)
Why Northern Hemisphere summer is longer (~93 days) than NH winter (~89 days)
Practical implication: NH receives slightly less solar energy in summer despite longer duration
Connection to the concept of 'equation of time' and sundial inaccuracies

concepts.name: Astronomical vs. Meteorological Seasons: Definition Conflict
key_dimensions: Astronomical seasons defined by solstices and equinoxes
Meteorological seasons defined by temperature records (Dec–Feb = winter in NH)
India's IMD season classification (4 seasons) vs. global 4-season model differences
Why meteorological seasons lag behind astronomical seasons (thermal lag of land/ocean)

concepts.name: Thermal Lag and the Warmest/Coldest Month Anomaly
key_dimensions: Why July (not June 21) is the hottest month and January (not Dec 22) the coldest in NH
Ocean's high specific heat causing greater thermal lag in coastal vs. continental regions
Southern Hemisphere thermal lag patterns and their comparison with NH
Implication for monsoon onset and withdrawal timing in India

concepts.name: Apparent Movement of the Sun (Solar Declination) Throughout the Year
key_dimensions: Sun's declination moving from 23.5°S (Dec 22) to 23.5°N (Jun 21) and back
Twice a year, the Sun is overhead at every latitude between the tropics
Zenith Sun passing over India: implications for seasons and Indian monsoon trigger
UPSC trap: On which dates does the Sun rise exactly due East and set due West (equinoxes only)

concepts.name: Milankovitch Cycles: Long-term Seasonal and Climatic Variation
key_dimensions: Three cycles: Eccentricity (100,000 yrs), Axial Tilt/Obliquity (41,000 yrs), Precession (26,000 yrs)
How precession ('wobble') changes which hemisphere faces Sun at perihelion over millennia
Role of Milankovitch cycles in triggering Ice Ages — distinction from short-term seasonal change
UPSC trap: Milankovitch cycles explain past climate change but NOT current anthropogenic warming

concepts.name: Precession of Equinoxes: The Wobble Effect
key_dimensions: Earth's axis wobbles like a spinning top with a 26,000-year cycle
In ~13,000 years, NH summer will coincide with perihelion (currently it's winter)
Historical shift: 'Vernal equinox' was once in the constellation Aries (now Pisces)
Distinction between precession and axial tilt change — both are separate Milankovitch cycles

concepts.name: Circle of Illumination: Geometry and Seasonal Shift
key_dimensions: Circle of illumination always bisects the equator but does NOT bisect other latitudes (except equinox)
On June 21: entire area within Arctic Circle (66.5°N–90°N) is in daylight; Antarctic Circle in darkness
Relationship between circle of illumination tilt and axial tilt (they are complementary)
UPSC trap: Circle of illumination passes through both poles only on equinox dates

concepts.name: Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) Migration and Seasons
key_dimensions: ITCZ follows the thermal equator which migrates with the overhead Sun position
ITCZ shift northward in NH summer drives the Indian Summer Monsoon
Why ITCZ migrates more over land than ocean (land heats/cools faster)
Seasons near the equator defined by ITCZ passage — two wet and two dry seasons (not temperature)

concepts.name: Seasons at the Poles: Extreme Manifestations of Earth's Revolution
key_dimensions: Six-month polar day and night as the most extreme seasonal expression
Despite 24-hour sunlight in Arctic summer, temperatures remain low due to low angle of incidence
Antarctic winter vs. Arctic winter: Antarctica colder due to continental landmass effect
Aurora Australis/Borealis — indirectly linked to seasons through solar wind interaction at poles

concepts.name: Indian Seasonal Calendar and Its Astronomical Basis
key_dimensions: IMD's four seasons: Winter (Jan–Feb), Pre-monsoon/Summer (Mar–May), SW Monsoon (Jun–Sep), Retreating Monsoon (Oct–Dec)
Traditional Hindu calendar's six seasons (Ritu) and their correspondence to solar declination
Why India's 'summer' (March–May) starts before the astronomical summer solstice (June 21)
Overlap trap: Retreating monsoon season vs. NE monsoon — same period, different terminology

concepts.name: Land and Sea Differential Heating: Seasonal Amplification
key_dimensions: Land heats and cools faster than water — creates extreme seasonal temperature contrasts in continental interiors
Maritime locations have muted seasons (smaller annual temperature range) vs. continental locations
Siberia as the extreme case: very hot summers, very cold winters despite similar solar input as Western Europe
This differential drives monsoons, land breezes, and sea breezes at seasonal scale

concepts.name: Solargraph and Analemma: Apparent Path of the Sun as Seasonal Evidence
key_dimensions: Analemma: figure-8 pattern traced by the Sun at the same time each day — combines declination and equation of time
Why the analemma is asymmetric (one loop larger) — linked to elliptical orbit (Kepler's 2nd Law)
Solargraph evidence: Sun's arc is higher in summer, lower in winter, directly proving seasonal change
UPSC application: interpreting Sun's path diagrams to identify season, hemisphere, and latitude
